This is Agropulse Open Mike. Republicans in the House of Representatives have spent the last few weeks searching for a new leader and a path for that leader to gain the necessary support in a chamber floor vote. Florida Republican Kat Kamak says aside from searching for the right candidate, the party might need to search for the right governing mindset as well.

I think that there are people who never left the campaign trail. Much of the same rhetoric that they used is easy on a campaign trail. It's the bomb throwing. It's the easy to digest sound bites. But governing is difficult. And with 218, you can do anything. But with such slim majorities, it's hard for people to get to that point. And so I think we have a lot of rebuilding of trust collectively as a conference that we need to do. But we also need to keep in mind that in this particular moment, we're up against a clock. We have tremendous implications that come with a shutdown. Many people think that the government shuts down and all the spending stops. Actually, it goes up in a government shutdown, which is one of the wild elements of government. And then of course you have a lot of the the back room deals that you know so many people are just sick and tired of. I know for me I am very sick and tired of the oh we had a deal or you promised me this and and it cuts so many ways across the conference that at this point in time I think that there needs to be a healthy dose of transparency. here in the Republican conference of things that people have asked for, things that people have requested of leadership. Put your money where your mouth is. If you want to be a chairman, put it out for the American public to see. If you want a hideaway capital office, put it out for the American people to see. Because at the end of the day, we're here to serve the American people. and the keeping of secrets is no longer and never has been in my book acceptable. So I think before I can even get behind a candidate, we need to see some fundamental changes to the way that business is conducted up here in Washington because the institution, it's fractured.

the House Freedom Caucus, and this is a group that has a lot of requests and a lot of thoughts when it comes to policy, not the least of which relate to agriculture. That all being said, What would be your council should the Republican leadership ask for it? On that Venn diagram between respecting the opinions and the views of the Freedom Caucus, but not allowing those opinions and views to have perhaps a bigger role in the operation of the House of Representatives than the membership size of the caucus might dictate.

Well, and I would even expand it beyond that. I think it's bigger than just the Freedom Caucus. You have so many factions, essentially we're operating within coalition government. There's so many different, they call us the five families. I would venture to say there's more factions than just five, including a group of free agents, of which I consider myself to be one. It's important that leadership, particularly with these numbers, and not just even in this particular Congress where we have such a slim majority, but in all, all Congresses, they respect every member in their opinion, because at any moment, particularly these times where social media is so dominant, You can have a member who will say and do something completely extravagant and wild and do it for clicks and views and shares and small dollar donation fundraising. I call it the anger-tainment model that many of my colleagues have adopted. But I would say, having experience with the Freedom Caucus, part of the challenge is that being a member of the Freedom Caucus means that you have to turn your vote card over to the group. You have a requirement as a member of Freedom Caucus to not only pay thousands of dollars to join the organization, but then you have to vote with them 80% of the time. My constituents back home in Florida's third, they own my voting card. No group, no other member, no specialty interest group has my voting card. Only my constituents control my voting card. In large part, one of the reasons why I am not a member, but I am considered Freedom Caucus adjacent. To that end, many of my friends are members. And as I talk to them on AG issues, I continually come back to, historically, the Freedom Caucus has voted in a large block against the Farm Bill. And of course, we can all talk about the nutritional side of where the lion's share of spending goes towards. In this case, the Farm Bill that we're working through is 82% nutritional. And you just take a step back from that, the amount of money that's going into the actual food production and the people who are putting the food on the shelf versus the people who are taking the food off the shelf, it is just fundamentally unbalanced. And for so many producers around the country, it's becoming an untenable situation. So I ask my Freedom Caucus friends to think of the Farm Bill as a national defense strategy, because a nation that cannot feed itself is not secure. And so rather than trying to attack food production and farm programs that are the very basic safety nets, the very basic elements that allow people who have so much skin in the game and so much risk out in the fields. I asked them to think of it in those terms rather than how it has been framed over the years and I would say even decades at this point of corporate subsidies. So I think that that's an element of the discussion that we need to be talking about when we're talking about my conservative friends, because I have a lot of conservative friends that are supporting the Farm Bill, but particularly when it comes to House Freedom Caucus, they have stood in opposition to it.

Personally, I would like to advocate for a voluntary base update with certain commodities. because I recognize that a base update across the board would blow the caps and we just don't have the money for that. turn_text: Let's stay in the weeds for a second then and

about the base update because there's obviously a lot of folks that have looked at that conversation from a Midwest versus a Southern versus a Western perspective for Northern Florida. Walk me through what a base update means and what particular commodities are we talking about here that stand to perhaps gain or maybe lose some base acres.

I use the term voluntary deliberately because I believe under a voluntary base update that has the potential to be a win-win situation for a lot of different commodities and producers. If you do a mandatory, I think that's when you start seeing caps blown out, that's where you start seeing winners and losers, and we don't want to do that. I think that there is a bit of a symbiotic relationship between the reference price increase and a base update, a voluntary base update. In my case, for example, we have peanuts in my part of the world where to the north and to the west, you have most of the peanuts being grown on base acres. for my young farmers coming up, they don't have the same level playing field. They're coming at this from a disadvantage, and they have to plant thousands and thousands more acres just to even compete on the scale of those that have base. And so I even go so far as to say that this campaign to engage in a voluntary base update, even scheduling out the commodities, because we certainly don't want this to turn into a turf war situation. between the Midwest producers and the Southeast. That's not it at all. I think that this entire campaign and move to do this really is about the young farmers. We talk at length about how are we going to get the next generation involved and anyone who is even close to agriculture knows that this next generation of farming families has at least one real estate agent. that is out there selling off pieces of the family farm. That's true in Florida, that's true in Texas, that's true all across the country. And it's because you have to be at such a scale and it's so capital intensive that it's virtually impossible to make a living in agriculture today unless you were born into it. So for me this is about supporting that next generation giving them a fighting chance and really doing what we should have been doing all along is a regular schedule of updating the base acreage. I think peanuts, cotton, rice would be a great start. I think because of the budgetary constraints that we're operating within it makes sense to schedule and scale this. I love my corn and soybean guys, but man, they would blow the caps by just blinking at a base update. And so I think that that's something that we can play with and really look to do a schedule that would have a long-term look at this. But if we don't do that, I think that even a reference price increase has no impact on the producers in my neck of the woods. And being the lone Republican who represents all of Florida agriculture in the House of Representatives, This is something that's critically important to my producers who are diversified, who don't have base, who are looking to really establish themselves as that next generation. So I think that there's a path forward. It's just going to be a little bit in the weeds and we have a lot of educating to do along the way.

turn_text: As we come into the home stretch of our conversation, let's shift things over to broadband, in particular the idea and the concept of rural broadband. As you talk to your constituents in maybe some more rural parts of your district, do they have the connectivity they need?

I don't think anyone has the connectivity they need if you're in rural America today. I mean, my goodness. It's wild to me that we have invested $42 billion and over 136 programs dedicated to addressing the broadband issue in America and Congress and government just can't seem to get out of their own way. You have over building in certain areas and then none in others. One of the things that has been particularly frustrating is the regulatory environment where you have USDA and FCC all competing with each other, talking over each other, state maps competing with federal maps, private companies who are keeping their proprietary infrastructure to themselves, which I understand. But at some point, we all have to pull out a map and say, okay, where we built out and where we not. And I think some of the solutions have been while while intentioned, they have missed the mark in many ways. Artoff auctions, for example, is a great example of a lot of money spent and not a lot of action. And with a time frame of 10 years to produce a viable connection, well, that's just horseshit, in my opinion. I don't know if I can say that word on this, but that's how I talk, so. It's been 20 minutes and I haven't said a curse word, so that's progress for me. But it's wild to me that in 2023, we do not have every single American connected to high speed, reliable, and affordable internet. I think what the co-ops have been doing here as of late is really the path forward, where you have in the 1920s and 30s the electrification of America. That is really the moment that we're looking for with broadband and I think it's going to be our local co-ops that do that in rural America. They have a connection to every home and every business. They can deliver better, faster and cheaper than some of our bigger competitors and providers. And for areas where that's not a viable option, particularly as we're talking about high tech ag and precision agriculture, we can be relying on low orbit satellite connectivity like Starlink. I think that in conjunction with a wireless option, in addition to the dark fiber, that is really the trifecta of how we can make this work. And I'll use Central Florida Co-op in my own district as an example. They're offering services of 100 gigs up and down for 60 bucks a month. And they're connecting 250, 300 homes a week. And they have figured out a way to do it without federal assistance. That, I think, is the path forward, which really is a shame because taxpayers have now been put on the hook for so many billions of dollars, but it tends to get lost in all the red tape.
